entries.title: Stone
entries.summary: Fifteen loose cobbles are all the workable stone the island has. Knapped into blades and tool heads, they slowly wear away.

sections.text: Seven cobbles lie in the grass, and eight more sit loose in the rocky outcrop to the east: look at one and press [key]E[/key] to pry it free. That is all there is. The outcrop, the flat stone and the boulders are part of the island and can't be taken, and the bedrock under the soil can't be dug.

list: [b]Knapping[/b]: strike one stone with another to shape a cutting blade, an axe head or a digging blade. The hammerstone in your pack isn't used up; the stone you shape is.
[b]Fire[/b]: stones set around a fire bed block the wind and hold some of its heat in.

sections.text: Every blow knocks off flakes that are gone for good, and a stone that snaps leaves less to work with. A worn-out blade is gone entirely; a worn-out axe or digging tool gives back its handle and a dull, shapeless stone. Treat every cobble as precious.

sections.tip: Decide on the form before your first strike, rough it out with a few heavy blows, and finish with light taps. Most wasted stone comes from heavy blows struck too late.

entries.title: Wood
entries.summary: All wood comes from the great tree: its branches, limbs and trunk, and what it sheds. It regrows - but only as fast as the tree can grow.

list: [b]Twigs and sticks[/b]: a few lie under the tree from the start, and the tree drops a twig every several hours while it grows.
[b]Leafy branches[/b]: cut from the tree with a blade. Cut up, each gives two sticks, three twigs and a handful of leaves.
[b]Large limbs[/b]: chopped off with an axe. Each gives two poles, three sticks, two firewood, two twigs and two handfuls of leaves.
[b]Logs[/b]: only from felling the trunk. Split them into boards and firewood.

sections.text: Wood fresh off the tree is green and full of water. Green wood hisses and steams in a fire and burns poorly. Leave it lying in the open and it seasons - a day or two of sun and wind dries it. A wooden item's description says whether it is green, drying or seasoned, and rain wets it again.

Fuel, of course - but also tool handles, the fire drill, charcoal, and nearly every building: poles, sticks and boards hold up platforms, walls, roofs and ladders. Wood won't compost; it would take years to rot. Burn it or build with it.

The tree regrows what you cut, using sunlight, the island's air, and the water and nutrients around its roots. A branch takes at least ten in-game hours to grow back, a limb at least a day, and neither grows at all if the tree has nothing left to grow with. A felled trunk takes days to come back. See [b]The great tree[/b].

entries.title: Grass, straw and fiber
entries.summary: Cut grass, straw, plant fiber and leaves: the soft materials for tinder, cordage, thatch, bedding and compost.

sections.text: Grass covers most of the island. Pull it by hand - hold [key]LMB[/key] on a grassy patch with empty hands - or cut it far faster with a blade. Fresh cut grass is a green for the compost heap. Lay it down in the open and it cures into straw in about a day of fair weather; rain sets it back.
Straw is the island's best tinder: it catches at a lower heat than anything else. It is also the thatch for roofs and the stuffing of sleeping mats. Every grain sheaf you thresh gives a bundle too.

Fiber grass grows in clumps around the pond. Harvest a full-grown clump with [key]E[/key] for four to six bundles of long fiber, a few seeds and some cut grass. Two bundles twist into a length of cordage; three dry bundles are tinder for the fire drill. Wild clumps grow back after harvesting, and the seeds let you plant more.
The tree drops leaves now and then, and every branch and limb you cut up gives some. They make poor, smoky fuel but excellent compost.
Lawn grass grows back slowly on moist ground that hasn't been tilled or dug away. Fiber grass and grain can be farmed. All of these rot down into compost, and their nutrients go back to the soil.

entries.title: Soil and earth
entries.summary: Forty centimeters or so of soil over bedrock: where crops grow, water soaks in and nutrients live. Dug up, it becomes earth for filling holes, building mounds and daubing walls.

sections.text: Soil covers the island about forty centimeters deep - nearly sixty under the great tree - thinning to a few centimeters over the clay bank and to nothing in the pond. Under it runs a thin seam of clay, and under that, bedrock you can't dig. Altogether the island holds some 65,000 liters of soil: plenty, but not a liter more will ever be made.

Aim at bare ground and hold [key]LMB[/key]. With empty hands you have to pull the grass off first; after that each scoop moves about a liter. A digging tool goes straight through the grass and moves around three liters a scoop. Every four liters becomes one load of earth in your pack.
list: You can't dig right at the edge - the ground would crumble away.
You can't dig under the pond's water.
You can't dig among the tree's roots, right beside rocks or the mossy log, or under a building.
[b]Filling[/b]: hold a load and press [key]LMB[/key] on the ground to pack it back - into a hole, or to raise a spot.
[b]Charcoal mounds[/b]: earth packed over a burning woodpile seals it. See [b]Charcoal[/b].
[b]Wattle walls[/b]: earth (or raw clay) is daubed onto the woven sticks.

sections.text: Earth you dig carries no nutrients with it: they stay in the ground where it came from. For how soil feeds plants, see [b]Soil and fertility[/b].

sections.warn: Dig too deep and you reach clay, then bare rock, and nothing grows without soil. Put earth back when you are done with it.

entries.title: Clay
entries.summary: A bank of clay lies by the pond. Dug, kneaded with water and shaped, it becomes pottery - but the island will never make more of it.

sections.text: On the south-east side of the pond the grass gives way to a low, flat bank. There, only a few centimeters of soil cover a bed of clay up to forty centimeters deep. Clay also lies close under the soil along the pond's shore, and a thin seam of it runs beneath the whole island.

Hold [key]LMB[/key] on the bank. The first scoops bring up the thin topsoil, as earth; then you reach the clay. Bare hands bring up nearly half a liter of clay a scoop; a good digging tool, about three times as much. Every quarter liter becomes a lump of raw clay, damp with water drawn from the ground around it.

list: [b]Pottery[/b]: knead it with water into prepared clay, shape vessels, dry them and fire them.
[b]Wattle walls[/b]: raw clay can be daubed onto walls instead of earth.

sections.text: The bank holds roughly two thousand liters of clay - thousands of lumps - and none will ever form again. It doesn't vanish either: clay left lying dries out, and an unfired pot left in the rain slumps back into lumps of raw clay that you can work again. Only firing changes clay for good.

sections.tip: Prepare clay right by the pond: kneading needs splashes of water, and without a vessel the pond is the only place to get them.

track.text: Dig four lumps of raw clay
